Messages.Body:
Hello All,

I'm wondering what everyone thinks about the ranking system:

http://206.65.59.246/VTES/member.tpl

I have several complaints with the current system:

- The system was changed without soliciting ample feedback from the
players (as far as I know.)

- The ranking/rating system means nothing to most players (as far as I
know.)

- The current system very poorly reflects the difference between 2nd
place and last place at a table. In a tournament setting, it's
important to get Table Wins, but 2nd place compared to last place at a
table is also important.

- There is an entirely separate ranking system for Limited
Tournaments; I guess that's good, but there is apparently only 1
person in the world who has played more than 9 Limited tournament
games, so why bother?

- Most importantly, the current system doesn't recognize the
difference between these two situations: 0.5-0.5-0.5-0.5-0.5 vs
5-0-0-0-0, assuming you're not the player who got 5 VPs. That is, in
both situations you would be given a "loss" in the ranking system, but
one situation is much worse than the other.

I realize the ranking system isn't an issue with a simple answer; we
care about the likelihood of winning an individual game, and also the
likelihood of winning an entire tournament. The current system
focuses greatly on Table Wins, and I think it overlooks other aspects
of good play.

As a solution, I propose the following:

*************************************
* Go back to the old rating system. *
*************************************

That solution solves all of the above problems, and gives an elegant,
all-encompassing formula for all games. I think the only drawback of
the rating system is that it didn't overly stress Table Wins.

Perhaps other people can come up with a better hybrid solution.

Finally, please note that I am currently the #1 ranked player in the
world, so I'm only writing all this because I really think the system
is flawed and I'd like to see it improved. No one can accuse me of
saying the system is bad simply because I'm not doing well. :)

Ira Fay

Hello All,

I appreciate Robert's response; I didn't realize that the previous
system was unmanageable. I'm surprised that was the case since chess
players have been doing it for a long time, but I'll simply accept it
as true.

Most of my complaints have been addressed, but I do have one that
remains:

- The current system doesn't take into consideration the difference
between:
a) No table win for me, and someone else gets the Table Win
b) No table win for me, and no one gets the Table Win

In a tournament setting, there is a big difference between (a) and
(b). The current system considers both an equally bad loss, when in
fact one is much worse than the other.

Therefore, I propose the following change to the current rating
system:

***************************************************************
* If a player places first or tied for first at a table but *
* doesn't earn a table win, that game is counted neither as a *
* win nor a loss for that player. Career Games and VPs are *
* increased, but his Games and Wins do not change. *
***************************************************************

I think the above change addresses my primary complaint with the
system, and actually balances it better to reflect skillful play at a
tournament.

Also, I think the Paris rating system has some good ideas, but I
think it will need to be playtested and balanced quite a bit. Also,
it heavily favors players who play in big tournaments often, and not
everyone is able to do that.

I don't think this is really quite so relevant. If you're playing a
slow, wall type deck and your prey plays Setite S&B, chances are the
S&B deck is going to start rolling, perhaps sweeping. Taking second
place (being last person ousted), says nothing about how well you
played, just how lucky you got in table seating. If you get 1 VP, that
is normally sufficient to show you earned 2nd place. Isn't that
enough?

> - Most importantly, the current system doesn't recognize the
> difference between these two situations: 0.5-0.5-0.5-0.5-0.5 vs
> 5-0-0-0-0, assuming you're not the player who got 5 VPs. That is, in
> both situations you would be given a "loss" in the ranking system, but
> one situation is much worse than the other.

As above, this flaw has less to do with the ratings system itself, but
with time limits imposed on games. Anyone can "stall" out a game, or
play defensively to preserve their position "earning" 0.5 VPs. You
know much less about the outcome of a game seeing a string of 0.5 VPs
than a sweep with 5 VPs (obviously, since the game never "really"
concluded).

> I realize the ranking system isn't an issue with a simple answer; we
> care about the likelihood of winning an individual game, and also the
> likelihood of winning an entire tournament. The current system
> focuses greatly on Table Wins, and I think it overlooks other aspects
> of good play.

I personally think "Game Wins" are very important. I understand this
even more after playing Assamite combat exclusively in tournaments
(4-5 constructed plus 3 storylines), for the past 8 months. There's
almost no way an Assamite deck can be expected to sweep a table. It
does happen, but almost always requires a quirk of seating
arrangements to be remotely possible. There are a handful of occasions
where I took Game Wins at 5-player tables with only 2 VPs. In fact,
most combat decks will end up splitting VPs with someone else at the
table as a matter of course. Until I played combat extensively, I
didn't realize how crucial "table management" is success with a
non-weenie combat deck.

Of the proposals I had seen in other threads, the ones I liked most
did not require a arbitrary points scale (e.g. 10 points for 1st,
Triple points for "big" events). The best ones seemed to have some
sort of "bonus" inherent to the number of participants in the event.
That often is a better indicator of the quality of play at an event,
though of course, where there is wheat, there is chaff.

I think a couple of factors could be added to the current ranking
system which would give it a bit more credibility.

1) Calculate an average "Tournament Points" per game. Like you mention
above, this gives you some information about how a player finished
individual games. I still wouldn't over-emphasize this metric since
table seating affects this one most greatly, IMO.

1) Calculate an average # of participants for each player based on the
tournaments they attended. You could generalize that all else equal,
the player who participated in bigger events is more skilled than the
person who was in smaller events.

2) Continuously raise the bar for "career games" in order to achieve a
ranking. If you filtered the "Top Ranking" on those with 20+ or 30+
career games, you'd probably get a better picture of who performed the
best on a consistent basis. I'd venture that 50+ games is probably
where you'd have to be for the impact of individual games to have
minimal impact on a player's ranking, and this should probably be the
largest number on which to filter. On the web site, there could also
easily be a filter for "all rated players" who had 10 or more career
games so everyone could see where they stand.

4) Calculate a parallel rank for "Premiere Events" or perhaps
"Invitational Events." These would be all the Regional/Country
qualifiers or continental championships. The only problem doing this
is (particularly for Invitationals) is that there simply aren't a lot
of data points since these events are infrequent.

If White Wolf decides to use rankings for invitations, all of the
above measures, as well as those on the web site should be temporally
filtered based on whatever arbitrary time frame they choose (I'd pick
2 years). This will give players plenty of time to establish their
ratings and it would take into account changes in a person's skill
level (or VTES collection!) over time.

Overall, I don't think the system needs to be radically changed, but I
do think there is lots of information available in the tournament
results that can give us a better idea of how a person ought to be
ranked. It's just a matter of crunching the numbers.

> that get ousted before you.Hence, you get more TP. However,it don't

No, as far as I can tell, you are mistaken. Tournament points are
just an arbitrary tie-breaker system that measures nothing except
gives certain finishing positions which score the same number of
victory points in a game an edge over certain other finishing positions
in which the same number of victory points were score. For example,
a player finishing with zero victory points in a game ending with the
winning player sweeping (5-0-0-0-0) gets more tournament points than
a player who finishes with zero victory points in a game in which someone
else besides the winning gets at least one victory point (4-1-0-0-0).
That's all tournament points ever did, as far as I know.

Fred

I strongly disagree. The only real problem is to systems that *don't*
compare quality of opponents.

> Why go to the trouble
> of measuring the quality of opponents when we know that, in some areas, the
> same 5 people play against each other over and over again?

I'm really confused about the issue you have with it. The ELO system
(and I assume others, though I'd have to analyze the system in question
to decide for myself) certainly is no worse off for lack of crossover.
And it will correct for differential ability to the extent it can. If
you've got a totally isolated group of players who have never played outside
their population, then ELO can do nothing about reckoning the quality of
one set of players vs. the others and will spit out ratings based on how
well players do within their own group. I don't really see the problem
with this as long as everyone understands the limitations of the system.
(Obviously, you can't make predictions about a thing if you have zero
relevant data to work from.) To the extent there is cross-play, ELO
will correct for it - permanently draining points out of a worse-than-
average group of players and permanently sucking points into a better-
than-average group. Again, if the amount of cross-play is low then the
relative ratings may not get corrected as much as they should but what can
you do?

So to answer your question directly: normally, the same five people do *not*
play against each other over and over again so measuring the quality of
opposition is a highly worthwhile endeavor. And with regard to the
degenerate case, you do it anyway because that's how the system works and
it's more work than it's worth to simplify it for situations that are rare
exceptions.

> Under the current system, the statistics ignore the quality of opponents.
> This is similar to some professional sports statistics. Things like
> baseball's lifetime batting averages don't take into account the quality of
> the opponents in that division or league or whether or not the player played
> most of their games against lesser teams.

Frankly, I think that's a pretty lousy analogy. Although in a technical sense,
it's possible that some batter may only ever bat against the mop up relievers
and never the ace starters or the closers, that never happens in real life.
At least, not for players who play for very long. Professional sports leagues
are rather homogenous in terms of talent and each team plays all the others
on a regular basis so all the players will generally face a representative
cross-section of the talent in their league. Not so VEKN tournaments. One
player may play only against his rather modestly-talented local group for
years while another may travel to all the most competitive tournaments in
the world - and this precisely identifies the problems with your statistics.
In any case, the comparison thus fails in a very substantive way.

Fred

I'm not sure who you are or what you're talking about, but an ELO system
was in use up until last spring. Would have worked fine, too, had decent
coefficients been chosen. The problem you refer to is hardly insurmountable.
The answer used was to rank each player in a game in order of victory
points scored and create player-pair results by comparing the number of
victory points each scored. So if a game ended 3-1-1-0-0, the player
finishing with three points "won" against the other four players, the two
players scoring one point apiece "lost" to the player scoring three points,
"won" against the two players scoring zero points, and tied one another.
The two players ousted without a victory point tied each other and lost
to the other three. (Thus, in a five player game, 10 player-pair results
were scored. In a four player game, 6 player-pair results would be scored.)

That part worked just fine. The logistics were the real issue, as discussed
elsewhere.

No they don't. Not the *same* five players over and over. Even small local
areas usually have more than five players or it's not worth bothering
with tournaments. Since different games have different sets of players,
player quality needs to be taken into account or you have (as we do now)
meaningless numbers.

As for Jyhad, it's not all that "strongly local". Players travel
all the time and even limited contact allows the ELO system to adjust for
strong areas and weak areas.
